title: The Half-Light Weather
premise: Yara Galloway, once the most feared restaurant critic in Lagos and London, lost her sense of taste after a betrayal she has never named in print. When Mama Efua, the last fluent speaker of Nkọrọ—a dying language of her coastal hometown—asks Yara to become her final student, Yara returns to the delta town where her family's hotel empire was built on a buried wrong: her grandfather's theft of the language itself, recorded and sold as 'authenticity' for his resorts. As Yara learns Nkọrọ word by word, she discovers the recordings her family still profits from, and must choose between protecting her brother's inheritance and telling the truth that will end both the language's silence and her own. In the end, Yara publishes the story under her own name, loses everything but her voice, and speaks the first Nkọrọ sentence at Mama Efua's funeral—taste returning to her mouth like rain.
about_author: Sebastian Okafor is the pen name of a former food writer who spent a decade covering West African coastal communities before turning to fiction. The Half-Light Weather is their second novel, written partly in the estuary towns where oral archives are still kept in biscuit tins and memory.

chapters.title: The Critic Who Tasted Nothing
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. A lavish tasting menu in London passes over her tongue like wet paper; she files a glowing review she doesn't mean. We learn she hasn't tasted anything in five years and has survived by writing beautifully around the hole. Emotional beat: elegant numbness, the cost of performing a self.

chapters.title: A Letter in a Dying Tongue
chapters.summary: Yara receives a letter from Mama Efua, written in Nkọrọ script she half-recognizes from childhood, asking for one final student before the speaker dies. Her editor offers her a career-defining assignment on endangered languages—the perfect cover for going home. Beat: dread disguised as opportunity.

chapters.title: The Return Tide
chapters.summary: Yara arrives in the delta town of Ilase, now ringed by Galloway Grand Resorts. Her brother Dele runs the empire smoothly and greets her with warmth edged in ownership. POV alternates briefly to Dele, who sees her return as either reconciliation or threat. Beat: home as a place that remembers you differently.

chapters.title: First Words
chapters.summary: Mama Efua begins lessons in her kitchen: greetings, names, the word for rain that falls without darkening the sky—half-light weather. Yara can hear the language perfectly but cannot produce its tones; her mouth refuses. Beat: humility, the body keeping old secrets.

chapters.title: The Hotel Archive
chapters.summary: Dele shows Yara the resort's 'Heritage Wing,' where her grandfather's 1960s field recordings of Nkọrọ songs play on loop for tourists. Yara recognizes Mama Efua's young voice among them—and realizes the family has been selling the language for sixty years. Beat: cold recognition.

chapters.title: What Grandfather Recorded
chapters.summary: Yara finds her grandfather's notebooks in the archive: he paid speakers in rice and salt, never told them the recordings would be commercial property, and erased their names. Mama Efua's mother is listed only as 'Informant B.' Beat: inherited guilt made concrete.

chapters.title: Dele's Ledger
chapters.summary: Dele's POV. He knows about the recordings' provenance and has buried it deeper than his grandfather did; the Heritage Wing funds everything, including his daughter's school fees. He offers Yara a consultancy to 'curate' the archive properly—silence dressed as stewardship. Beat: corruption as ordinary bookkeeping.

chapters.title: Tones
chapters.summary: Lessons deepen. Mama Efua teaches that Nkọrọ meaning lives in tone—the same syllable means 'truth' or 'wound' depending on pitch. Yara finally produces her first correct phrase and tastes salt on her tongue, the first flavor in five years. Beat: breakthrough, fragile joy.

chapters.title: The Almost-Review
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter, Yara's POV: five years ago she discovered the resort group's flagship restaurant served stolen recipes from a dead cook whose family was never credited. She wrote the review, then pulled it under pressure from her then-lover, an editor with Galloway ties. Her taste left that night. Beat: the wound revealed.

chapters.title: Informant B's Daughter
chapters.summary: Yara asks Mama Efua about the recordings. The old woman already knows whose granddaughter sits in her kitchen; she chose Yara deliberately—not for forgiveness, but because a thief's heir owes the debt. Beat: confrontation softened by purpose; anger with a curriculum.

chapters.title: The Festival Booking
chapters.summary: The resort announces a Nkọrọ Cultural Festival featuring the archived recordings, with Mama Efua as 'honored guest.' Dele needs her living presence to authenticate the brand. Mama Efua agrees to attend—but tells Yara she intends to speak there, whatever it costs. Beat: ticking clock installed.

chapters.title: Salt and Silence
chapters.summary: Yara drafts an exposé and deletes it twice. Her editor calls wanting the festival piece; Dele senses her drift and warns her gently that the family survives by not saying things. Yara realizes she has spent her whole life practicing the art of almost saying it. Beat: the loyalty-truth vise tightens.

chapters.title: Night Lessons
chapters.summary: Mama Efua's health fails; lessons move to her bedside. She gives Yara the forbidden register of the language—the words used only for settling debts between families—and makes Yara promise to use them when the time comes. Beat: transmission, mortality, sacred trust.

chapters.title: The Buyer
chapters.summary: A heritage-tourism conglomerate offers to buy the Galloway archive outright, contingent on clean provenance papers. Dele forges them. Yara finds the forged document and understands that exposure now would destroy him criminally, not just reputationally. Beat: stakes escalate from shame to ruin.

chapters.title: Half-Light Weather
chapters.summary: A windless, grey day on the estuary. Yara and Mama Efua sit where Informant B once sang. Mama Efua says she does not want the language preserved—she wants it used, even once, by someone who owes it. Yara finally speaks a full paragraph of Nkọrō aloud. Beat: quiet center of the book; clarity.

chapters.title: Brother's Keeper
chapters.summary: Yara confronts Dele with the forged papers. He breaks: he knew what their grandfather did, and he built his life on the knowing. He begs her to wait until after the sale. She cannot promise. Beat: love and truth pulling in opposite directions; no villains, only costs.

chapters.title: The Pull
chapters.summary: Yara writes the full story—the recordings, the erasures, the forgery, her own silenced review—and sends it to her editor under her real byline, scheduled to publish the morning of the festival. Then she walks into the resort to face what she's done. Beat: point of no return.

chapters.title: Festival of Ghosts
chapters.summary: Climax, part one. On stage before investors and townspeople, Mama Efua takes the microphone and, instead of the rehearsed blessing, names Informant B—her mother—and accuses the Galloway name in Nkọrọ, translated line by line by Yara standing beside her. Beat: public rupture, terror and release.

chapters.title: What the Story Cost
chapters.summary: Climax, part two. The exposé publishes hours later. The sale collapses; regulators circle; Dele stops answering her calls. Mama Efua suffers a stroke that night. Yara keeps vigil, holding the words she was taught like something breakable. Beat: victory indistinguishable from loss.

chapters.title: The Last Speaker's Quiet
chapters.summary: Mama Efua dies at dawn, lucid long enough to hear Yara recite the debt-settling register back to her and answer, 'Now you owe no one.' Yara tastes rain on the air—real taste, faint but hers. Beat: grief transmuted into inheritance received.

chapters.title: Byline
chapters.summary: Aftermath. The archive is transferred to a community trust Yara helps found; Dele, stripped of the company, sends her one message in imperfect Nkọrọ—an apology, tonally wrong but legible. Yara resigns from criticism and begins teaching the language to three children in Ilase. Beat: rebuilding on honest ground.

chapters.title: Half-Light, Full Voice
chapters.summary: Final chapter, Yara's POV. At Mama Efua's funeral, Yara delivers the eulogy entirely in Nkọrọ, stumbling, corrected gently by the children. Afterwards she eats her mother's pepper soup at a roadside stall and tastes every layer of it. She writes one sentence in her notebook: 'I am the student.' Beat: resolution—voice, taste, and debt all settled.
